passage: The monsoon had flooded the underpass, so Sunaina reached the construction firm's office forty minutes late, soaked to the knees, on the one morning it mattered most. Three weeks ago she had written to the project head that the scaffolding inspections on the Kharghar site were being signed without anyone climbing up. Work there had stopped the same day while the scaffolds were re-checked. The concern was fixed, but she wasn't forgiven. Now her name was missing from the site list on the notice board. Her desk had been moved beside the photocopier. At the tea counter, the conversation stopped when she walked up. Nazia, who used to share her lunch every day, suddenly remembered a call and left. On the group chat, someone had forwarded a line from the project head: "Some people care more about complaints than delivery." Sunaina read it standing up, dripping, her throat tight.

qa.q: Where had Sunaina's desk been moved?
qa.a: Her desk had been moved beside the photocopier.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she read the forwarded line?
qa.a: Sunaina felt hurt and humiliated, her throat tight, seeing her honest report turned into an attack on her reputation.

qa.q: What turning point could Sunaina reach for now?
qa.a: Sunaina could write down each change since her report, with dates, and quietly reach out to anyone she still trusts, inside or outside the firm, for support and proper advice.

qa.q: Why might Nazia have left the tea counter so suddenly?
qa.a: Nazia may be afraid of being seen with Sunaina and blamed too, and possibly guilty about avoiding a friend.

grounding: Shows a person who raised a safety concern being sidelined and publicly blamed, with colleagues avoiding her out of fear.

passage: Layla had been the only one in the Toronto lab to report that the drug trial data had been cleaned up before submission. Since the review, nobody sat with her at lunch. Xin watched it every day from the next bench: Layla eating alone by the window, the team's weekend plans made loudly in front of her, the jokes about "our compliance officer." Xin had seen the same altered spreadsheet. Xin had said nothing, and every lunch felt heavier for it. On Friday, Xin stopped at Layla's bench on the way out and said quietly, "What you did took courage. If the review needs another person who saw the spreadsheet, I'll give a statement." Layla looked up, eyes wet. On Monday, Xin carried two coffees to the window table and sat down. Two other colleagues glanced over. By Wednesday one of them had joined.

qa.q: Where did Layla eat alone every day?
qa.a: Layla ate alone by the window.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling while watching Layla eat alone?
qa.a: Xin felt guilty for staying silent after seeing the same altered spreadsheet, and every lunch felt heavier for it.

qa.q: Which small acts of support made a difference here?
qa.a: Xin's quiet word of respect, the offer of a witness statement and simply sitting with Layla at lunch changed the mood, so another colleague joined.

qa.q: What is it like for Layla when Xin speaks to her on Friday?
qa.a: Layla is moved and relieved, eyes wet, to learn she is not completely alone after weeks of being shunned.

grounding: Shows a colleague who feels guilty at staying silent while a truth-teller is shunned, and small acts of support that shift the atmosphere.

subtype: Stage 6: External reporting and legal advice [Response]
passage:
"You've read the file three times, Bhupen. Tell me what the lawyer said," Trisha said, pouring tea for her brother.
"She said stop writing 'they're poisoning the village.' Write facts. Dates, readings, who I told and when."
"And the pollution board?"
"She's helping me file with them this week. She explained there are protections for people who report in good faith, and how they work."
"Good. Because your manager's 'we'll look into it' was two months ago."
"Three months. The effluent is still going into the canal. I checked on Sunday." He tapped a page. "Here. Sample date, reading, the photo, the email I sent on the fifth."
"No opinions?"
"Not one. She crossed out every adjective."
Trisha laughed. "Even 'disgusting'?"
"Especially 'disgusting.'"
She sat beside him. "Whatever happens next, you're not doing it alone. I'll come with you to the board."

qa.q: What did the lawyer tell Bhupen to stop writing?
qa.a: She said to stop writing they're poisoning the village.

qa.q: How is Bhupen feeling as he taps the page?
qa.a: Bhupen feels steadier and more determined now that he has clear facts, though frustrated that three months have passed with the effluent still flowing.

qa.q: Why is it wise for Bhupen to use facts instead of opinions?
qa.a: Dates, readings, photos and emails are hard to dismiss, so the report to the pollution board is stronger and more credible.

qa.q: How does Trisha see her role now?
qa.a: Trisha sees herself as Bhupen's support, keeping him company and offering to go with him to the board so he doesn't face it alone.

grounding: Shows a person turning to a lawyer and the proper authority after internal action fails, documenting facts rather than opinions and learning about protections.

passage:
Ramesh's diary, Saturday
The regulator's report came out this morning. Everything I flagged about the hostel kitchen's fire exits was in it, page four, in plain words. The company has to fix all three buildings.
I thought I'd feel like dancing. Mostly I feel tired, as if eighteen months of holding my breath all came out at once. I'm still not back at a job I like. Two old colleagues still don't answer my calls.
But Ankita made kheer without saying why, and my sister sent a photo of page four with a single heart. Suresh from the old team messaged, "You were right. I'm sorry I kept quiet." I cried a little at that one.
Tonight I walked past the hostel and saw the new exit sign lit up green. Some student will run out that door one day without ever knowing. That's enough. I'm proud of it, even on the tired days.

qa.q: On which page of the report was everything Ramesh flagged?
qa.a: It was on page four, in plain words.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Ramesh describe after the report?
qa.a: Ramesh feels exhausted and drained after eighteen months, yet also proud and quietly vindicated, especially at the green exit sign.

qa.q: What is helping Ramesh through this long tail?
qa.a: Support from Ankita, the sister and Suresh's apology, along with pride in having acted on conscience, helps even while the job and some friendships remain hard.

qa.q: How might Suresh feel after sending the apology?
qa.a: Suresh probably feels guilty for staying quiet and relieved to finally say so, hoping to repair some trust.

grounding: Shows the mixed tiredness and vindication after whistleblowing, sustained by support from people close by and pride in acting on conscience.

passage: The community centre's back room was empty on a Tuesday evening, which was why Tarun had suggested it. Tanvir sat across from his old college mentor with a folder on his knees. "I haven't told anyone at work. Not yet." Tarun nodded. "Good. Start with what you saw, not what you think it means." Tanvir opened the folder: a dated list of ration-supply deliveries that the NGO had recorded but the villages never received, with copies of the delivery slips. "I'm scared," he admitted. "My father's surgery is next month, and I'm the only earner." Tarun didn't tell him to be brave. "Then plan around that. Keep your notes at home, not on the office laptop. Talk to the lawyer from the legal-aid clinic I mentioned, in confidence, before you file anything." Tanvir let out a long breath. "So waiting a week isn't cowardice?" "It's preparation. It'll make your report stronger."

qa.q: What did Tanvir's folder contain?
qa.a: It held a dated list of ration-supply deliveries the NGO had recorded but the villages never received, with copies of the delivery slips.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel when he says waiting a week might be cowardice?
qa.a: Tanvir feels scared and a bit ashamed, worried about his father's surgery and about seeming weak for not acting at once.

qa.q: What makes Tarun's guidance a strong turning point?
qa.a: Tarun helps Tanvir record facts, protect his notes, plan around family needs and speak to a lawyer in confidence, so any report is careful and stronger.

qa.q: How might Tarun see his role as a mentor here?
qa.a: Tarun likely sees himself as a steady, private sounding board, helping Tanvir think clearly without pushing him into risk.

grounding: Shows an employee speaking in confidence with a trusted mentor, recording facts and dates and weighing family needs, treating preparation as strength.

subtype: Stage 1: The hurt and the anger [Actor]
passage: "Tanuja, your face is exactly like mine was at fifteen. Sit with your Zubin Mama and listen. My best friend then was Behram. We shared everything. One evening I told him I was scared of the dark, still, at fifteen. The next morning, the whole class was making ghost noises at me. Behram was laughing with them. I remember my ears burning, my hands shaking. I wanted to throw my geometry box at him. I didn't; I walked out and sat behind the school water tank until the bell. My mother found me angry at dinner and said, 'Good. You should be angry. He broke your trust.' That surprised me. I thought anger was wrong. It wasn't. It was telling me something important had been crossed. What I did with it came later. But the anger itself, beta, that was honest."

qa.q: Where did Zubin sit until the bell?
qa.a: He sat behind the school water tank until the bell.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when the class made ghost noises?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and furious, with burning ears and shaking hands, because Behram had shared his secret and laughed.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point came from Zubin's mother's words?
qa.a: By telling Zubin his anger was right, his mother helped him see it as a sign that trust had been broken, not as something wrong with him.

qa.q: How might Behram have felt when Zubin walked out?
qa.a: Behram may have felt a flash of guilt or awkwardness, realising his joke had deeply hurt his best friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager betrayed by a friend who shared his secret, feeling rage and humiliation, and learning that the anger signals a crossed boundary.

passage:
Dear Jyoti Didi,
You said to write when my head gets too full, so here goes.
It's been two weeks since Sanya showed my diary pages to her new friends. I keep replaying it. The exact look on her face. What she said, "It's just funny, Noor." I lie in bed and have whole arguments with her in my head, and in them I always win. I say something so sharp that everyone turns to look at her instead.
Sometimes I plan things. Like posting that embarrassing video of her from the picnic. I don't do it. But thinking about it feels good for a minute, like I have power again. Then it's 1 am and I'm still awake and my stomach hurts.
I don't think I'm getting over it. I think I'm just getting stuck.
Please call on Sunday?
Love,
Noor

qa.q: How long has it been since Sanya showed the diary pages?
qa.a: It has been two weeks since Sanya showed Noor's diary pages to her new friends.

qa.q: How does imagining payback make Noor feel?
qa.a: It makes Noor feel powerful for a moment, but then hurt, sleepless and stuck, with a stomach ache at 1 am.

qa.q: What could Jyoti Didi suggest on Sunday's call to help Noor move forward?
qa.a: Jyoti Didi could listen to how hurt Noor is, then help Noor notice that the replaying keeps the pain fresh and find ways to set the imaginary arguments down.

qa.q: How might Jyoti Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jyoti Didi may feel protective and worried, but glad to be trusted with it, and keen to call on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a betrayal, imagining payback and rehearsing arguments, and feeling the thoughts keep the pain fresh.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' block, Sunday evening
Arohi has been storming about Tanuja for two weeks, since Tanuja moved rooms and told everyone Arohi was "impossible to live with." She slammed doors, told anyone who'd listen, and ripped their shared photo off the corridor board.
Tonight I found her in the common room with the torn photo in her lap. She wasn't angry. She was crying quietly. She said, "We were going to share a flat after college. She knew about my father. She was the first person here who knew me." Then: "I'm not even angry anymore. I just miss her."
What I did next: I sat with her and didn't hurry her. I told her missing someone who hurt you is normal, and that this sadness is part of moving on. I made her tea and let her stay in the common room as long as she wanted. I've suggested she see the college counsellor this week if the sadness keeps weighing on her.

qa.q: What did Arohi rip off the corridor board?
qa.a: She ripped their shared photo off the corridor board.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling underneath her anger?
qa.a: Arohi found deep sadness and grief for the lost friendship and the future flat, missing the first person at the hostel who really knew her.

qa.q: What did the warden's response offer Arohi at this point?
qa.a: The warden stayed without rushing her, named the sadness as a normal part of moving on, and suggested the counsellor if it keeps weighing on her.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see things if she heard Arohi now misses her?
qa.a: Tanuja might feel surprised and perhaps sad too, since her words about Arohi came from hurt of her own.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding grief for a lost friendship beneath her anger and allowing the sadness, which moves forgiveness forward.

subtype: Stage 4: Seeing the other as human [Actor]
passage: I'm Abhinav. Last semester Zainab submitted our joint project under her name only, and I lost the internship it could have got me. For months I called her a thief in my head. Then, last week, at the college canteen, her roommate told me something I didn't know. Zainab's scholarship depended on that grade; if she lost it, she'd have to leave college and go back home. She had panicked the night before the deadline. Hearing that didn't make what she did okay. It was still wrong, and I still lost something real. But I noticed something change in me. She stopped being a villain and became a scared person who did a bad thing. The bitterness I'd been carrying loosened a little, like a knot finally let go. I don't know if I'll talk to her yet. I just don't hate her the way I did.

qa.q: What did Zainab's scholarship depend on, according to her roommate?
qa.a: Zainab's scholarship depended on that grade.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel after hearing about Zainab's scholarship?
qa.a: Abhinav still felt wronged, but his bitterness loosened, as if Zainab had become a frightened person instead of a villain.

qa.q: What is Abhinav's next possible step now that the bitterness has eased?
qa.a: Abhinav could decide calmly whether to talk to Zainab, naming what her act cost while understanding her fear, without pretending it was okay.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt the night before the deadline?
qa.a: Zainab was probably panicked and desperate, terrified of losing the scholarship and being sent home.

grounding: Shows a young adult beginning to understand the wrongdoer's fear and circumstances without excusing the act, and bitterness loosening.

subtype: Stage 4: Seeing the other as human [Observer]
passage: The overnight bus from Pune to Goa had broken down somewhere in the ghats, and the passengers sat on the roadside wall in the drizzle while the driver waited for a mechanic. Pema had heard Ishita's story four times now: how Ishita's college roommate had read her messages and shown them to the whole class group. Each time the story got a little more bitter. Pema had a line ready, the one everyone says: just forgive her and move on. She swallowed it. Instead she passed Ishita the last packet of biscuits and just listened, nodding, until the words ran out. The rain dripped off the bus roof. After a long pause Pema asked, gently, "What do you want now? From her, or for you?" Ishita stared at the dark road for a while. "I think," she said slowly, "I want to stop carrying her with me everywhere."

qa.q: Where did the bus break down?
qa.a: The bus broke down somewhere in the ghats.

qa.q: Why did Pema swallow the line about forgiving and moving on?
qa.a: Pema felt it would sound dismissive to someone still hurting, and cared more about Ishita feeling heard than about fixing it.

qa.q: Why did listening first and then asking a question work better?
qa.a: It let Ishita empty out the bitterness without being rushed, then think about what she wanted for herself, which moved her forward.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita when Pema asks what she wants now?
qa.a: Ishita is surprised into thinking beyond the story, and for the first time she names a wish to stop carrying the hurt around.

grounding: Shows a friend hearing a bitter story again and again, listening first and then gently asking what the person wants now instead of telling them to forgive.
